exploreSites.name: Dolly Varden Mine
overview: The Dolly Varden is a documented mine within the Alma district and Mount Bross mining landscape.
Federal mapping and mineral-interest records preserve it as a distinct named property rather than a generic label for nearby workings.

timeline.text: Colorado Geological Survey Bulletin 3 treated the Dolly Varden within its study of the Alma district’s geology and ore deposits.

USGS mapping continues to identify the Dolly Varden Mine on the Alma quadrangle.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey and USGS records independently preserve the mine’s identity and district context.

moreHistory: History Colorado and Park County records establish the complex and distinguish its principal components.

exploreSites.name: Buckskin Joe / Laurette / Buckskin
overview: Buckskin Joe, originally called Laurette, was one of Park County's earliest gold-rush settlements and briefly served as the county seat.
The camp grew around placer and lode gold mining, then declined rapidly as the richest early deposits were exhausted.

timeline.text: The settlement was organized as Laurette during the early South Park gold rush.
A post office opened and the mining community expanded.
The county seat moved to Buckskin Joe.
The county seat moved to Fairplay as Buckskin Joe declined.

moreHistory: The original townsite should not be confused with the later tourist attraction that reused the Buckskin Joe name.

The standing mill represents the later phase of a property whose mine history reaches back to the 1880s and whose ore-processing system changed repeatedly as operators tried new technology.

Fire destroyed the earlier mill.
A replacement mill was completed and resumed ore treatment.
Mining and milling ceased during wartime shortages.

overview: Montgomery was an early Park County mining town established after placer-gold discoveries near the base of Mount Lincoln.
The settlement supported numerous nearby mines and developed hotels, taverns, and other businesses before the mining boom faded.

timeline.text: Montgomery was established during the early South Park gold rush.
A Montgomery post office was established as the town expanded.

moreHistory: The historic townsite and nearby mine landscapes should be treated separately from later reservoir development.

exploreSites.name: Orphan Boy Mine
overview: The Orphan Boy was a gold-and-silver mine in Mosquito Gulch near Alma, at the east foot of Loveland Mountain.
Colorado Geological Survey records place it within the Buckskin subdistrict of the greater Alma mining district and describe vein-and-manto mineralization in the Sawatch Quartzite.

timeline.text: EPA records identify the Orphan Boy as a gold-and-silver discovery from the opening years of the Alma district.
The Colorado Geological Survey compilation reports that more than 11,000 tons had been produced, while the exact lifetime total remains uncertain.
EPA carried out a removal action addressing mine-related environmental hazards.
EPA recorded completion of the removal action.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey RS-40 and its Patton, Hoskin & Butler source trail document the mine’s geology and district setting.
EPA independently preserves the mine’s identity, commodity history, approximate elevation, and modern cleanup record.
Historic production figures are presented only as reported by the geological compilation; no modern reserve or grade estimate is inferred.

production.summary: Historical sources document gold, silver, and associated base-metal ores; no definitive lifetime production total is asserted.

commodities.name: Base-metal ores
commodities.period: Associated mineralization documented by the Colorado Geological Survey

exploreSites.name: Paris Mill & Paris Mine
overview: The Paris Mill processed gold-, silver-, and lead-bearing ore from the Paris Mine and nearby Buckskin Gulch workings.
Its surviving machinery and engineered systems make it one of Colorado’s comparatively intact examples of a late-nineteenth-century ore-processing mill.

timeline.text: South Park National Heritage Area records the discovery of the Paris Mine.
Preservation sources describe construction beginning in 1894, while state and county records support completion in 1895.
The mill was adapted with flotation equipment as processing methods changed.
Major operations permanently closed.
The Paris Mill was listed in the National Register of Historic Places for its mining-industry significance.

moreHistory: An aerial tram linked the mine and mill, reducing ore-transport costs in Buckskin Gulch.
History Colorado and Park County records document successive changes to the mill’s processing systems.
The construction sequence is retained as 1894–1895 rather than forced to a single year because preservation sources differ on start and completion.

features.name: Paris Mill
features.note: The preserved mill and machinery are the principal interpretation focus.

features.name: Paris Mine Relationship
features.note: The mine supplied ore to the mill through an aerial-tram relationship.

identificationSites.name: Boston & Colorado Smelter
identificationSites.location: 90 N. Main St., Alma, Park County, Colorado
overview: The Alma branch of the Boston and Colorado Smelting Company was completed in 1873 to treat ore from mines on Mounts Lincoln and Bross. Park County landmark records support its identity, surviving location, and importance to Alma's early mining economy.

identificationSites.name: Hilltop Mine
identificationSites.location: Upper eastern slope of the Mosquito Range, Park County, Colorado
overview: Hilltop was the most productive documented mine in the Horseshoe district and was linked by a long aerial tram to the Leavick mill. USGS and Colorado School of Mines sources support the identity and location while preserving uncertainty over the reported discovery date.

identificationSites.name: Leavick Mining Town & Hilltop Mill
identificationSites.location: Fourmile Creek / Horseshoe Gulch, Park County, Colorado
overview: Leavick was a mining settlement and mill center on Fourmile Creek closely tied to the Hilltop operation, its aerial tram, and short-lived railroad service. Archival and architectural-history sources support the identity and location; conflicting mill-construction dates remain intentionally unresolved.

identificationSites.name: Mosquito Pass Mining Corridor

This record covers the corridor itself; named mines, mills, and camps along it remain separate components.
